title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
A fake think tank with no legal existence created over 560,000 words of content in nine days and placed it into platforms designed to influence AI chatbots. The content presented pro-Israel arguments on disputed topics including war crimes and genocide allegations, framed as neutral research. The operation was registered with the US Justice Department as foreign propaganda material but appears to have been deployed into AI training without disclosure of its origin or intent.

This shows a system failure at the point of data intake. AI chatbots draw from large training datasets that now contain material deliberately structured to manipulate their outputs, with the source of that material obscured. The content was seeded by contractors hired specifically to place it where machine learning systems would find it. What it would have taken to catch this is verification of the provenance and funding of sources before they entered training datasets, and scrutiny of whether sources claiming to be independent American research actually have legal existence and disclosed ownership.

It is not established whether the chatbots that consumed this material actually changed their responses as a result, or whether this operation had the effect its architects intended.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

A fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute for Public Policy, funded by the Israeli government, published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days using a platform designed to influence artificial intelligence chatbots. The institute, which has no legal existence or physical address, presented pro-Israel arguments on controversial topics including alleged war crimes and genocide claims, framing them as neutral research. The reports were structured as questions users might ask AI systems and heavily relied on selective sourcing to obscure criticism of Israel's actions. The operation was registered with the US Justice Department as Israeli government propaganda material.

This effort is part of a larger campaign financed by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government and routed through European advertising firm Havas Media. Multiple American contractors, including Clock Tower X run by former Trump digital director Brad Parscale, were hired to place content into AI training databases where chatbots draw information. Israeli officials have publicly expressed frustration that these expensive public diplomacy campaigns have failed to improve Israel's standing in American public opinion, with recent polling showing Americans increasingly sympathize with Palestinians and view Israeli military actions unfavorably.
